newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia c.bank law could seal division - experts.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia c.bank law could seal division - experts.

text.p: An agreement on a draft central bank law could seal the ethnic partition of Bosnia because it fails to require the use of a single currency throughout the country, economists and diplomats said on Friday.
"This directly undermines the last hope for a unified Bosnia through the monetary system and a unified Bosnia altogether," one foreign economic expert told Reuters.
A U.S. delegation announced a deal on the central bank law on Thursday after seven hours of negotiations with Bosnia's Serb, Croat and Moslem leaders, ending six months of dispute over the issue.
The proposed law refers to an overall understanding that a new Bosnian currency should be employed in the country's two entities -- the Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic.
But the agreement allows Serb authorities to continue to use currency from neighbouring Yugoslavia for some official transactions in Serb-controlled territory.
The Serbs are supposed to eventually halt use of the Yugoslav dinar after a transition period but the compromise agreement set no deadline.

Under the proposed law, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will issue a report every three months to determine whether the Serb economy has acquired enough foreign exchange funds to join the Bosnian monetary system.
Once the IMF makes the recommendation, it will be up to the country's three-man presidency to make a decision and each member has the power of veto, including the Serb member Momcilo Krajisnik.
"He can veto it forever," said another expert, who asked not to be named.
Western experts in Sarajevo expressed deep concern over the agreement, saying it undermined peace-making efforts to bind the country together through economic links based on a single currency.
The draft law is to be put before the country's joint parliament for adoption probably in the first ten days of June, diplomats said.

"If it goes through the parliament, I would say this was a sell-out of unified Bosnia," a Western diplomat said. "Basically, we are accepting the status quo of the partition if you can't use the same money all over Bosnia."
Bosnian Serb separatists fought a bitter 3-1/2 year war against Moslems and Croats in a bid to form a union with the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.

The fighting ended with a peace accord in November 1995 but the Serb leadership has been actively obstructing international efforts to reunify the country. As a result, they received only two percent of more than one billion in foreign aid last year.
The U.S. negotiators clinched the central bank deal in the belief that international pressure will soon force the Serbs to discard Yugoslav dinars, diplomats familiar with the negotiations said.
"The option was to have something or to have nothing," he said.

The French governor of the central bank, Serge Robert, said on Thursday the law allows for a transition period because the Serb republic's economy is "so much integrated into the economy of Belgrade (Yugoslavia)".
Since Bosnia's peace treaty was agreed 18 months ago at a U.S. air force base in Dayton, Ohio, little has been achieved in stitching the country back together.
Few refugees have returned to their homes and newly-elected joint institutions have adopted legislation only under enormous international pressure and protracted negotiations.
Foreign experts had viewed a single central bank and currency as the main catalysts of unification.
"The central bank was the first test of unification under the Dayton accord and it failed the Bosnian people. That is shameful," the diplomat said.
